solutions.title: Import Price Anomaly Detection & Country Risk Clustering
solutions.description: Isolation Forest applied to 39,955 real UK customs import records — declared value and weight per shipment, queried live from HMRC's public trade API — flags unit prices that look statistically unusual for their product category, the same signal customs risk teams check for under- or over-invoicing. Cross-checked against an independent statistical rule rather than assumed correct: only about half the flags agree, an honest finding showing the two methods catch genuinely different things. K-Means then separates country-product pairs into risk tiers — one group of 41 pairs runs a 29% anomaly rate against 1.7% everywhere else.

narrative.label: The Challenge
narrative.text: Customs and trade-risk teams need a cheap way to flag which import declarations deserve a second look — without the one thing that would make it easy: labeled examples of confirmed fraud, which no customs agency publishes.

narrative.label: Real Data, Queried Live
narrative.text: 39,955 real import shipments — declared value in GBP and net mass in kg — pulled directly from HM Revenue & Customs' public Overseas Trade Statistics API. No account, no key: it's fully open government data. Four months of 2024, 19 commodity categories, 164 countries, nothing cherry-picked.

narrative.label: Comparing Fairly
narrative.text: A kilo of live animals and a kilo of electrical machinery are never on the same price scale, so unit price is standardized as a z-score within each commodity category before anything else happens — otherwise the model would just rediscover category price differences, not real anomalies.
narrative.caption: Real shipments, six categories: value vs. weight, flagged shipments in red — off the normal price line for their product.

narrative.label: Flagging the Outliers
narrative.text: Isolation Forest, trained jointly on standardized price and value, flags the 3% most unusual shipments — fully unsupervised, since no ground-truth fraud label exists to train against.
narrative.caption: Flagged shipments cluster at the tails of the real price distribution, exactly where they should.

narrative.label: An Honest Cross-Check
narrative.text: A second, independent method — a simple IQR rule on price alone, sharing zero logic with Isolation Forest — agrees with only about half of its flags. That's not a failure: it shows the two methods are genuinely catching different things. Isolation Forest weighs price and value together, so it catches combinations that look off even when price alone doesn't; the IQR rule catches the reverse. Reporting only the overlap that flattered the result would have been the dishonest version of this chart.
narrative.caption: 602 flagged only by Isolation Forest, 499 only by the IQR rule, 597 where both agree.

narrative.label: Grouping by Risk
narrative.text: K-Means groups country-commodity pairs by their average price deviation, anomaly rate, and shipment volume. One cluster of 41 pairs comes out with a 29.3% anomaly rate — seventeen times higher than the other 542 pairs at 1.7%. That's not 41 confirmed fraud cases; it's 41 places a human reviewer's limited time would actually be well spent.
narrative.caption: K-Means (k=2, silhouette-selected) — a small, sharply distinct high-risk cluster separates cleanly from the rest.

narrative.label: Why It Matters
narrative.text: Every published customs-fraud model with strong accuracy numbers was trained on confirmed fraud labels held internally by a national customs agency — data nobody outside that agency ever sees. This is the honest version available to everyone else: no ground truth to train against, only internal consistency checks and a defensible way to prioritize where scarce review time goes.

study.code_spotlight:
# Standardize price WITHIN category -- never compare raw prices across products
df['z_price'] = df.groupby('category')['log_price'].transform(
    lambda x: (x - x.mean()) / x.std())

iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, contamination=0.03, random_state=42)
df['anomaly'] = iso.fit_predict(df[['z_price', 'z_value']]) == -1
# 1,199 / 39,955 flagged (3.0%) -- only 49.8% also flagged by an independent IQR rule

# K-Means on country x category risk profile
km = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=42)
# Cluster 1: 41 pairs, 29.3% anomaly rate vs. 1.7% everywhere else

solutions.title: Fetal Health Risk Detection & Clustering
solutions.description: An unsupervised pipeline that flags at-risk fetal heart-rate patterns and groups 2,126 real cardiotocogram recordings into risk tiers — without ever seeing the clinical diagnosis. Isolation Forest anomalies concentrate 12x more in cases obstetricians independently classified as pathological (48.9% vs. 4.1%), and K-Means recovers a high-risk cluster where pathological cases outnumber normal ones. A real early-warning signal, built entirely from the signal itself.

narrative.label: The Challenge
narrative.text: Real clinical monitoring produces a dense stream of numbers per patient — heart rate, variability, contractions — that even trained clinicians have to read holistically, in real time. Could an algorithm that never sees the diagnosis still learn to spot what actually matters?

narrative.label: The Data
narrative.text: 2,126 real cardiotocogram recordings, each independently classified Normal, Suspect, or Pathologic by a consensus of expert obstetricians (Ayres-de-Campos & Bernardes, 2000). That diagnosis was set aside completely during modeling — it comes back later, only to grade the work, never to train on.

narrative.label: Finding What's Unusual
narrative.text: An Isolation Forest was trained on the 20 raw measured features per recording — never the diagnosis — and asked one question: which recordings look structurally different from the rest? The red points below are everything it flagged.
narrative.caption: Isolation Forest anomalies, 2,126 recordings in PCA space — the model never saw a diagnosis.

narrative.label: Did It Actually Work?
narrative.text: Only after the model made its decisions did we compare its flags against the real diagnoses. Recordings doctors called Pathologic were flagged anomalous 12x more often than recordings they called Normal — a gap this wide doesn't happen by chance.
narrative.caption: Anomaly rate by real clinical diagnosis, checked after the fact.

narrative.label: Grouping by Risk
narrative.text: A second, independent model — K-Means — sorted every recording into one of three groups, again with zero access to the diagnosis. One group came out almost entirely Normal. Another inverted the dataset's own risk ratio: inside that one cluster, Pathologic cases actually outnumber Normal ones.
narrative.caption: K-Means (k=3) — real diagnosis composition per cluster, revealed only afterward.

narrative.label: An Honest Extra Check
narrative.text: We also compared the flagged anomalies against a real external clinical threshold — ACOG's normal fetal heart-rate range. They barely overlapped. That's not a failure: it shows this multivariate model catches risk patterns a single clinical rule alone would miss, instead of just rediscovering what a simpler check already knows.

narrative.label: Why It Matters
narrative.text: None of this replaces a doctor. What it demonstrates is that a fully unsupervised model, given only the raw signal, independently rediscovers real clinical risk — a legitimate, honest early-warning layer worth building on, not a black box asked to take over.

study.code_spotlight:
# 1. Anomaly detection — unsupervised, never sees NSP
iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, contamination=0.08, random_state=42)
df['anomaly'] = iso.fit_predict(X_scaled) == -1

# 2. Clustering — validated post-hoc against the real diagnosis
km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42)
df['cluster'] = km.fit_predict(X_scaled)

# 3. External validation — did the model rediscover real clinical risk?
pd.crosstab(df['anomaly'], df['NSP_label'], normalize='columns') * 100
# Pathologic: 48.9% flagged anomalous  |  Normal: 4.1% flagged anomalous

solutions.title: Automated Haul Truck Dispatch Planning for Open-Pit Mining
solutions.description: A PDDL domain and optimal planner routing open-pit mine haul trucks from extraction benches to the mill or waste dump over a one-way haul-road network — the same real dispatch problem behind the DISPATCH® system used across the mining industry since 1986, now solved with provable optimality instead of a heuristic rule. The same domain handles three growing scenarios unchanged, and adding a second mill actually shortens the optimal plan — the planner found and used a dedicated shortcut on its own.

narrative.label: The Challenge
narrative.text: Open-pit haul truck dispatch — which truck goes to which pit, which one delivers to the mill or the dump — is a real, decades-old mining operations problem, not a toy example. Model it as a classical planning problem and get a provably optimal answer instead of a heuristic dispatch rule.

narrative.label: Modeling a Real Mine Layout
narrative.text: One-way haul roads, exactly like real open-pit traffic control that keeps loaded and empty trucks off the same bench road: trucks leave the yard, reach a pit, pick up ore or waste, and deliver — ore only accepted where a location is marked as a mill, waste only where it's marked as a dump.

narrative.label: Solving It — Provably
narrative.text: Two trucks, two pits, one mill, one dump. A* with the LM-Cut admissible heuristic doesn't just find a route — it proves this is the cheapest one possible: 10 actions, mathematically optimal.
narrative.caption: The full haul-road network, one-way loops, the dedicated pit-c → mill2 shortcut highlighted in gold.

narrative.label: Scaling It Up, Without Touching the Model
narrative.text: A third pit and a second ore load were added — the exact same domain file solved the bigger scenario too. Zero modifications to the model itself, plan length grows to 16 actions.
narrative.caption: Optimal plan length across three growing scenarios — same domain.pddl, unchanged.

narrative.label: The Interesting Part
narrative.text: A second mill was added with its own dedicated short haul road from one specific pit. The optimal plan for that harder scenario is actually shorter than the simpler one before it — 15 actions instead of 16 — because the planner independently discovered and used the shortcut for that pit's ore, while routing the other pit's ore the normal way. Nobody told it to prefer it.

narrative.label: Why Pyperplan, Not Fast Downward
narrative.text: The related rover-planning project in this portfolio runs Fast Downward inside a Singularity container. This one deliberately used pyperplan — a pure-Python planner, zero container or Linux dependency — because A* with an admissible heuristic gives the same provable-optimality guarantee either way. The tool changed; the guarantee didn't.

pipeline: 🗺️ Modeling: PDDL domain — move / pick-up / deliver-ore / deliver-waste, generic for any number of mills or dumps
⛏️ Scenario 1: base case — 2 pits, 1 mill, 1 dump — 10 steps optimal
🪨 Scenario 2: +1 pit, +1 ore load — 16 steps optimal
🏭 Scenario 3: +1 mill with a dedicated shortcut — 15 steps optimal, planner used the shortcut on its own
✅ Solved with pyperplan, A* search + LM-Cut admissible heuristic — provably optimal, not heuristic
study.code_spotlight:
(:action deliver-ore
    :parameters (?t - truck ?l - load ?loc - location)
    :precondition
    (and
        (at ?t ?loc)
        (carrying ?t ?l)
        (ore ?l)
        (mill ?loc)
    )
    :effect
    (and
        (delivered ?l)
        (free ?t)
        (not (carrying ?t ?l))
    )
)

; python -m pyperplan -s astar -H lmcut domain.pddl problem3.pddl
; -> Plan length: 15 (optimal) -- planner routes pit-c's ore via the shortcut to mill2

solutions.title: Automated Mission Planning for Autonomous Rovers
solutions.description: A PDDL domain and optimal planner (Fast Downward, A* + LM-Cut, run in a Singularity container) that plans multi-stop rover routes over a directional path network — provably optimal every time, verified independently against a second planner. The same domain.pddl handles three growing scenarios without a single line changed, and in the hardest one the planner independently chose the closer of two labs for each delivery.

narrative.label: The Challenge
narrative.text: A rover has already excavated two mineral samples at two different sites. Bad weather stopped it from moving them. Plan the route that gets both to the analysis lab — over a path network where some roads only go one way.

narrative.label: Proving the Pipeline First
narrative.text: Before writing a single line of the actual problem, the exact tool chain — a Singularity container running Fast Downward — was verified against a real competition task, pulled directly from the official IPC 2018 repository, rather than trusted blindly.

narrative.label: Modeling the Problem
narrative.text: The rover's world becomes three PDDL actions: move between connected locations, pick up a mineral, deliver it to any location marked as a lab — deliberately generic, never hardcoded to one specific lab.

narrative.label: Solving It — Provably
narrative.text: Run against the real path network from the brief, the planner doesn't just find a route — it proves this is the shortest one possible: 14 steps, mathematically optimal.
narrative.caption: The real directional path network from the problem brief.

narrative.label: Scaling It Up, Without Touching the Model
narrative.text: Two new scenarios were added — another mineral and site, then a second lab entirely — and the exact same domain file solved both. Zero modifications to the model itself.
narrative.caption: Optimal plan length across three growing scenarios — same domain.pddl, unchanged.

narrative.label: The Interesting Part
narrative.text: In the hardest scenario, with two labs available, the planner independently chose to deliver each mineral to whichever lab was actually closer — proof the model generalizes on its own, rather than happening to work by coincidence.

narrative.label: Why Delfi 1 Isn't Here
narrative.text: The actual IPC 2018 champion planner, Delfi 1, is honestly unreachable today: its container lived on Singularity Hub (shut down in 2021), its source on a Mercurial repository (Bitbucket dropped Mercurial support in 2020). Since Delfi 1 is itself built on Fast Downward, this project runs Fast Downward directly — with the same optimality guarantee the competition's own optimal track requires.

pipeline: 🗺️ Modeling: PDDL domain — move / pick-up / deliver, generic over any number of labs
🧪 Pipeline validation: real IPC 2018 benchmark task (Snake), solved in 24 optimal steps
🪨 Problem 1: base scenario — 2 minerals, 1 lab — 14 optimal steps
🔬 Problem 3: +1 mineral, +1 lab — 18 optimal steps, planner chose the nearer lab per delivery
✅ Validation: every plan cross-checked against a second, independent planner
study.code_spotlight:
(:action deliver
    :parameters (?rover ?mineral ?loc)
    :precondition
    (and
        (at ?rover ?loc)
        (carrying ?rover ?mineral)
        (LAB ?loc)
    )
    :effect
    (and
        (analyzed ?mineral)
        (not (carrying ?rover ?mineral))
        (free ?rover)
    )
)

; Run to provable optimality:
; fast-downward.sif domain.pddl problem3.pddl --search "astar(lmcut())"
; -> Plan cost: 18 (optimal) -- planner delivers to whichever LAB is closer

solutions.title: Automated Pallet & Carton Counting from Images
solutions.description: A classical computer-vision pipeline that counts cartons on a pallet from a single top-down image — and an honest test of the standard published fix for the hardest failure case. When two cartons sit flush against each other, the textbook method (watershed segmentation, used successfully for counting fruit) does NOT recover the correct count, because rectangular cartons don't have the shape it depends on. The actual fix — reading the thin shadow seam between adjacent boxes — gets it exactly right, matching where the current 2025 research literature on this problem is heading.

narrative.label: The Challenge
narrative.text: A quick, honest question for any warehouse or import operation: how many cartons are actually on this pallet, counted straight from a photo, without touching a barcode scanner? Build the counting pipeline, then test it against the one case that actually breaks it — two boxes pushed flush together.

narrative.label: Building an Exact Ground Truth
narrative.text: Rather than a real warehouse photo (with no controlled way to know the true count), a synthetic top-down pallet image was generated — 30 cartons, randomized size, rotation, and position, with one pair deliberately pushed together with zero gap. The count is known exactly because it was drawn.
narrative.caption: Synthetic top-down pallet — 30 cartons, kraft-cardboard rendering, ground truth known exactly.

narrative.label: The Naive Count Falls Short
narrative.text: Otsu thresholding plus connected-component counting is fast and simple — and it undercounts by exactly one carton, because the two touching boxes merge into a single blob in the binary silhouette.
narrative.caption: Grayscale render, Otsu binary mask, and the naive connected-component count — 29 instead of 30.

narrative.label: Trying the Textbook Fix
narrative.text: Distance-transform watershed is the standard published method for separating touching objects — it's what makes fruit-counting and cell-counting research work. Applied here directly, not assumed to work, it still returns 29. The reason is structural: watershed finds a concave "waist" where two round objects touch, and two rectangles pushed flush together have no waist at all — their silhouette is just one bigger rectangle.
narrative.caption: Naive, distance-transform watershed, and edge-aware correction, side by side — only one gets 30.

narrative.label: What Actually Works
narrative.text: Two cartons touching still cast a thin shadow crease where their surfaces meet — a real physical cue a photo shows, invisible to a binary silhouette. Canny edge detection recovers that seam directly from the grayscale image and uses it to cut the mask before recounting.
narrative.caption: Zoomed on the touching pair — the textbook fix stays merged, the edge-aware correction splits it correctly.

narrative.label: The Result
narrative.text: 30 out of 30, exactly matching the ground truth — and getting there required knowing why the obvious fix doesn't apply to this shape of object, not just running more algorithms at it.
narrative.caption: Carton count by method: ground truth 30, naive 29, watershed 29, edge-aware correction 30.

narrative.label: Why It Matters
narrative.text: This runs on a single 2D photo, needs no training data and no GPU, and the current 2025 research on this exact problem is moving toward full 3D reconstruction specifically because flat images lose cues that matter for touching or occluded boxes — the same limitation this project hit directly, at a fraction of the complexity. That makes it a cheap, fast pilot to run against real pallet photos before deciding whether it's worth building further.

study.code_spotlight:
# Textbook fix for touching objects -- does NOT work for flush rectangles
dist = cv2.distanceTransform(binary, cv2.DIST_L2, 5)
# -> still 29/30: no concave "waist" between two flush rectangles

# What actually works: read the real seam, not the silhouette
edges = cv2.Canny(gray, 40, 120)
cut = cv2.bitwise_and(binary, cv2.bitwise_not(cv2.dilate(edges, kernel)))
n_labels, labels, stats, _ = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(cut)
# -> 30/30, exact match to ground truth

solutions.title: Impulse Noise Restoration & Contrast Enhancement
solutions.description: Two classical image-processing pipelines — median-filter denoising and contrast enhancement — built from scratch in NumPy and benchmarked against OpenCV rather than assumed correct. The from-scratch median filter matches OpenCV's restoration quality within 0.04 dB PSNR (94%+ MSE reduction) while running four orders of magnitude slower, which is exactly why production systems never loop over pixels in Python. A second, honest finding: gamma correction reliably brightens a dark image but doesn't reliably add contrast — only histogram equalization does that.

narrative.label: The Challenge
narrative.text: Two everyday image defects, two different fixes: impulse (salt-and-pepper) noise needs a filter that rejects outliers instead of averaging them in, and a genuinely low-contrast image needs its intensity range redistributed, not just brightened. Build both from the underlying math, then prove each one actually works — against a library, not just by eye.

narrative.label: Injecting a Known Corruption
narrative.text: 5% of pixels in two test images were forced to pure black or pure white, with a fixed random seed — a controlled, reproducible corruption rather than a real but unmeasurable one, so the recovery can be scored exactly.
narrative.caption: 5% salt-and-pepper noise injected into two test images.

narrative.label: Building the Filter From Scratch
narrative.text: A median filter replaces every pixel with the middle value of its 3×3 neighborhood — non-linear, so it excludes extreme outliers instead of blending them in the way a mean filter would. Implemented as a raw double loop over every pixel in NumPy, with reflect-padding at the borders.
narrative.caption: Noisy image, own median filter, and cv2.medianBlur — visually indistinguishable.

narrative.label: Checking the Work Against OpenCV
narrative.text: PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) against the clean original quantifies the restoration: the from-scratch filter and cv2.medianBlur land within 0.04 dB of each other on both images — the math is correct. The only real difference is speed: the naive Python loop took over 5 seconds per image against 0.13 milliseconds for OpenCV's sliding-histogram algorithm (Huang, 1979) — a ~40,000x gap that has nothing to do with correctness.
narrative.caption: PSNR before and after filtering — own implementation vs. OpenCV, camera and coins.

narrative.label: Finding Low Contrast Automatically
narrative.text: Rather than picking images by eye, six candidates were ranked by intensity standard deviation (σ), and the two lowest were treated as "low contrast" — moon (σ=13.3) and clock (σ=20.9) — then enhanced two ways: a from-scratch gamma (power-law) lookup table, and cv2.equalizeHist.
narrative.caption: Low-contrast originals vs. gamma correction (γ=0.4) vs. histogram equalization.

narrative.label: The Finding That Wasn't Forced
narrative.text: Gamma correction more than doubled mean brightness on both images (+39% to +63%) — but actual contrast (σ) didn't rise with it, and on one image it dropped. Histogram equalization was the technique that genuinely maximized contrast, boosting σ by 250–455%, because it redistributes the pixel distribution itself instead of remapping it along one fixed curve. Brighter and higher-contrast are not the same property, and only one of these two methods reliably delivers the second.

narrative.label: Why It Matters
narrative.text: Neither result was assumed — both were checked against an independent implementation and a real metric before being reported. That's the same discipline applied here that goes into every dataset this practice touches: build it, then verify it actually did what it claims.

study.code_spotlight:
def median_filter_own(image, kernel_size=3):
    r = kernel_size // 2
    padded = np.pad(image, pad_width=r, mode='reflect')
    output = np.zeros_like(image, dtype=np.uint8)
    for i in range(image.shape[0]):
        for j in range(image.shape[1]):
            window = padded[i:i+kernel_size, j:j+kernel_size]
            output[i, j] = np.median(window)
    return output

# Own filter vs. cv2.medianBlur: PSNR within 0.04 dB, ~40,000x slower

def gamma_correction_own(image, gamma=0.4):
    lut = np.clip(((np.arange(256) / 255.0) ** gamma) * 255.0, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
    return lut[image]
# Brightens (+39-63% mean) but does not reliably raise contrast (sigma)

solutions.title: Custom Certification & Training Platform
solutions.description: Many companies need to train teams on a specific tool, internal process, or compliance topic — and generic courses don't cover that. This is a self-paced trainer with spaced-repetition scheduling, built to turn any body of knowledge into a certification-style question bank that actually sticks, instead of a slide deck nobody reopens. I originally built it to stay sharp on my own technical fundamentals — because in this field, you either keep training or you fall behind.
